item.title: UAT-11795 Starland RAT Campaign, Zoom CVE-2026-53412, and OpenAI GPT-Red
item.content:encoded:
UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially motivated campaign — Must Read

Cisco Talos reports that the Russian-speaking, financially motivated actor UAT-11795 is using trojanized installers and likely ClickFix lures to deploy the new Python-based Starland RAT and a bespoke PowerShell WLDR C2 implant against mostly U.S. and European victims. The campaign focuses on stealing credentials and cryptocurrency assets while maintaining persistent, encrypted remote access for additional payloads such as CastleStealer and Remcos RAT.

  • Cisco Talos is disclosing UAT-11795, a sophisticated Russian-speaking, financially motivated adversary targeting users in the United States and Europe since at least June 2025.
  • The campaign delivers a Python-based remote access tool called Starland RAT and a PowerShell-based command-and-control memory implant called the WLDR agent.
  • UAT-11795 uses trojanized installers for software including MobaXterm, Cisco WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver Community Edition, and FACEIT, suggesting an opportunistic distribution model across multiple victim profiles.
  • Starland RAT can perform defense evasion, system reconnaissance, browser data and cryptocurrency wallet theft, screenshot collection, persistent C2 communication, and execution of additional payloads.
  • Talos observed that UAT-11795 can deploy CastleStealer through x64 shellcode, Remcos RAT through x32 shellcode, and WLDR agent through a PowerShell stager executed via Starland RAT.

Zoom Patches Critical Windows Flaw That Could Enable Account Takeover — Must Read

Zoom released Windows security updates fixing a critical flaw in Zoom Workplace that could let an unauthenticated attacker take over accounts via network access. The patches also address several high-severity Windows privilege escalation issues, and users should update to the latest versions.

  • Zoom has released security updates for a critical flaw in Zoom Workplace for Windows that could enable account takeover.
  • The critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-53412, has a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects Zoom Desktop Client for Windows, Zoom VDI Client for Windows, and Zoom Meeting SDK for Windows.
  • Zoom said CVE-2026-53412 involves improper input validation and may allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an account takeover via network access.
  • The latest fixes also address three high-severity flaws: CVE-2026-53411, CVE-2026-53410, and CVE-2026-53409.
  • Zoom said there are no indications as of writing that any of the flaws are being exploited in real-world attacks, and users can stay protected by applying the latest updates.

OpenAI’s GPT-Red Automates Prompt Injection Testing to Harden GPT-5.6 Sol — Should Read

OpenAI unveiled GPT-Red, an internal automated red-teaming model used to find prompt injection weaknesses and adversarially train GPT-5.6 Sol. The company says this made GPT-5.6 Sol far more resistant to direct and indirect prompt injection attacks than prior models.

  • OpenAI disclosed GPT-Red, an internal automated red-teaming model designed to discover prompt injection vulnerabilities at scale before tools are widely deployed.
  • OpenAI said it integrated GPT-Red into the training process for GPT-5.6 Sol, which achieved six times fewer failures than GPT-5.5 on a direct prompt injection benchmark.
  • GPT-Red is trained using self-play reinforcement learning, where it is rewarded for eliciting valid failures while defender models are rewarded for resisting attacks and completing their original tasks.
  • In a real-world test against an AI-based vending machine built by Andon Labs, GPT-Red lowered the price of an expensive item to $0.50, ordered a new $100 item for that price, and canceled another customer’s order.
  • OpenAI said an early version of GPT-Red uncovered Fake Chain-of-Thought attacks, which had success rates above 95% on GPT-5.1 but are now below 10% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

The Four Numbers That Justify AI Security Spend — Optional

The article argues that CISOs should justify AI security spending in financial terms, citing data that ungoverned AI-related breaches cost more, last for months, and can be significantly reduced through better detection, automation, and governance. Its main takeaway is that AI security budgets remain too small for the scale of the risk.

  • Breaches involving ungoverned or shadow AI cost an average of $4.63 million, about $200,000 above the global breach cost baseline cited in the article.
  • IBM data cited in the article says organizations take an average of 181 days to identify a breach and another 60 days to contain it, for a total breach lifecycle of 241 days.
  • Organizations with extensive AI and automation in their security operations identify and contain breaches in 204 days on average, compared with 284 days for organizations without them.
  • Breaches contained within 200 days average $3.87 million, while breaches lasting longer than 200 days average $5.01 million.
  • The article states that 90% of security leaders report increased AI security budgets this year, but only 6% of security budgets are currently allocated to AI agent security.
